stem: A manager runs a pooled fund into which investors contribute and from which they redeem at their own discretion. For the purpose of comparing this manager's performance against a peer group, the most appropriate return measure is the:
choices: money-weighted rate of return, because it reflects the actual growth of invested capital.
time-weighted rate of return, because it is not distorted by the size and timing of external cash flows.
internal rate of return, because it solves for the single rate that equates inflows and outflows.
solution: A time-weighted return chains sub-period returns, so it measures the return on a unit of currency left in the fund throughout. That is the right basis for comparing managers who do not control when investors contribute or redeem. A money-weighted return answers a different question: what the investor actually earned given their own timing.
distractors: This measures the investor's experience, which is the right question for a client report and the wrong one for ranking a manager who did not choose the cash flow dates.
The internal rate of return is the money-weighted return under another name, so it carries the same timing distortion.

stem: An investor buys a share for USD50.00, receives a dividend of USD2.00 at the end of the year, and sells the share for USD54.00. The continuously compounded annual return is closest to:
solution: The holding period return is (54.00 - 50.00 + 2.00) / 50.00 = 12.00%. The continuously compounded return is the natural log of one plus that figure: ln(1.12) = 11.33%. For a positive return the continuously compounded figure is always the smaller of the two.
distractors: This is the holding period return itself, before converting to a continuously compounded basis.
This is exp(0.12) - 1, which converts in the wrong direction.

stem: A sample of 100 monthly observations has a mean of 6.5% and a standard deviation of 2.0%. An analyst tests the hypothesis that the population mean equals 6.0%. The value of the test statistic is closest to:
solution: The test statistic is the difference between the sample mean and the hypothesised mean divided by the standard error. The standard error is 2.0% / sqrt(100) = 0.2%, so the statistic is (6.5 - 6.0) / 0.2 = 2.50. Against a two-tailed critical value of about 1.98 at the 5% level, the null would be rejected.
distractors: This divides by the sample standard deviation rather than the standard error, omitting the square root of the sample size.
This divides by a standard error expressed in the wrong units, inflating the statistic tenfold.
